proposition.claim:
A \(q\)-cluster includes the exterior cell; a single bubble therefore has \(q=2\). Individual cells need not be connected. In \(\mathbb R^n\) only the exterior cell has infinite volume. Total perimeter counts each interface once. Reflection symmetry means invariance of each labelled cell, not just invariance of the union of interfaces.

Definitions 2.26 and 2.28, printed p. 100 (PDF 30), require stationarity and \[\delta_X^1 V=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 Q(X)=\delta_X^2 A-\langle\lambda,\delta_X^2V\rangle\geq0
 \qquad (X\in C_c^\infty).\] Perturbations are not restricted to reflection-symmetric fields or to preserving each connected component’s volume.

Theorem 1.3 concerns bounded stable regular clusters with reflection symmetry. The stable-cluster extension in Theorem 1.9 additionally assumes connected total boundary and finitely many cell components. The global minimizing conclusion in Theorem 1.13 is \(2\leq q\leq\min(5,n+1)\). Statements 1.14 and 1.16 are explicitly announced without proof in this paper; they are not treated as completed proofs here.

Remark 9.14, printed p. 161 (PDF 91), proposes taking a stable \(q\)-cluster whose \(q-1\) finite cells lie in one open hemisphere and reflecting it about the equator. It states that the resulting \(q\)-cluster is stable and has disconnected cells, as an example showing why connectedness of the total boundary is needed in Theorem 1.9.

The suspect step is preservation of stability when a cell and its reflected copy receive the same label. The volume constraint then permits transferring volume between those two components.

Starting unit disk is standard stable bounded regular stationary2cluster; lies in openhalfplane. Reflected labelled pair is bounded regular stationary and S0 symmetric, q<=n+1, finitecomponents; stability is disputed conclusion, not assumed.
